blocks.text: Yet no one should hope that it can be concluded from this that in the words of Job רננים renanim are peacocks. For many reasons stand against it. The first [col. 242] is taken from history, both sacred and profane. For both teach that the peacock was first brought from India, long after the times of Job. In sacred history this is found in 1 Reg. X, 22. and 2 Paral. IX, 21.: Once in three years the fleet (of Solomon) came from Tarshish, bringing gold and silver, elephants' teeth, apes, ותכיים, and peacocks. None of the ancients renders the Hebrew word otherwise, as we said in its place ^{b)}. Moreover, there would have been no need to bring peacocks into Judaea from such distant regions if the Jews, or the Arabs neighbouring the Jews, had already had them long before. Now, if we consult the Greeks, Theophrastus, as cited by Pliny, reports that peacocks are imported into Asia. And Aelian, History of Animals, book 5, chapter 21: Λέγεται δὲ ἐκ βαρβάρων εἰς Ἕλληνας κομισθῆναι· καὶ χρόνου πολλοῦ σπάνιος ὢν, εἶτα ἐδείκνυτο τῶν ἀνθρώπων τοῖς φιλοκάλοις μισθοῦ. Καὶ Ἀθήνησί γε ταῖς [II, 843] νουμηνίαις ἐδέχοντο καὶ ἄνδρας, καὶ γυναῖκας, ἐπὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν αὐτῶν, καὶ τὴν θέαν πρόσοδον εἶχον. ἐτιμῶντο δὲ τὸν ἄῤῥενα, καὶ τὴν θῆλυν δραχμῶν χιλίων· ὡς Ἀντιφῶν ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἐρασίστρατον λόγῳ φησί. [Legetai de ek barbarōn eis Hellēnas komisthēnai; kai chronou pollou spanios ōn, eita edeiknyto tōn anthrōpōn tois philokalois misthou. Kai Athēnēsi ge tais noumēniais edechonto kai andras, kai gynaikas, epi tēn historian autōn, kai tēn thean prosodon eichon. etimōnto de ton arrena, kai tēn thēlyn drachmōn chiliōn; hōs Antiphōn en tō Pros Erasistraton logō phēsi.] It is said to have been brought from the barbarians to the Greeks; and since it was for a long time rare, it was at last shown to the curious for a fixed fee. And at Athens, when men and women were admitted to see it on the first day of the month, they made a profit from it. And they valued a male and female at a thousand drachmas, as Antiphon says in the Speech Against Erasistratus. This speech had another title, Περὶ ταῶν [Peri taōn], On Peacocks, as we learn from Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 12. But that title seems to have been added by someone else, for the author himself calls them nothing but ὄρνεις ποικίλους [orneis poikilous], variegated birds. Was it perhaps because the name ταῶν [taōn], then recent, he did not yet dare to use in a speech? Indeed ταὼς [taōs] is read in the Birds of Aristophanes, and in the Acharnians, Τοῖς ταῶσι [Tois taōsi]. But, besides the fact that Aristophanes was somewhat later than Antiphon, the rules of oratory and of comedy are different: comedy uses the words of the common people, oratory a polished and more correct style. However that may be, we learn from the same speech that peacocks had begun to be kept at Athens thirty years earlier, in the house of a certain Demus, son of Pyrilampes, καὶ πολλοὺς παραγίνεσθαι μετὰ πόθον τῆς τῶν ὀρνίθων θέας ἔκ τε Λακεδαίμονος, καὶ Θετταλίας [kai pollous paraginesthai meta pothon tēs tōn ornithōn theas ek te Lakedaimonos, kai Thettalias], and that many came (to Athens) from Lacedaemon and Thessaly out of desire to see these birds. From which you may infer that these birds then first began to become known to the Greeks. Nor can the age of Pyrilampes be uncertain, since Plutarch in the Pericles relates that he was a friend of Pericles, and even mentions his τὰς ὀρνιθοτροφίας, καὶ ταῶνας [tas ornithotrophias, kai taōnas], aviaries and peacocks. Accordingly, in the age of Alexander there were still few peacocks in Greece. And, on the testimony of Aelian, in the place cited above, Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Μακεδὼν ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἰδὼν τούσδε τοὺς ὀρνίθας ἐξεπλάγη, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους θαυμάσας ἠπείλησε τῷ καταθύσαντι ταὼν ἀπειλὰς βαρυτάτας· [Alexandros ho Makedōn en Indois idōn tousde tous ornithas exeplagē, kai tou kallous thaumasas ēpeilēse tō katathysanti taōn apeilas barytatas;] Alexander the Macedonian, seeing these birds among the Indians, was struck with admiration for their beauty and threatened the severest penalties on anyone who killed a peacock. Curtius too, in book 9, testifies that Alexander found wild peacocks near the Indian river Hydraotes: From here, he says, they came through deserts to the river Hydraotes. Adjoining the river was a grove shady with trees unknown elsewhere, and full of a multitude of wild peacocks. From this very passage one learns that the peacock came from India. Hence the same Aelian, as above, book 11, chapter 33: Ταὼν δὲ Ἰνδικὸν δῶρον λαβὼν ὁ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλεὺς ταὼν, ὡς ἰδεῖν, μέγιστόν τε καὶ ὡραιότατον· [Taōn de Indikon dōron labōn ho tōn Aigyptiōn basileus taōn, hōs idein, megiston te kai hōraiotaton;] When the king of Egypt had received as a gift an Indian peacock, a very large and very beautiful one. And book 13, chapter 18, where he describes the palace of the king of the Indians: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς παραδείσοις τρέφονται μὲν ταὼς ἥμεροι· [En de tois paradeisois trephontai men taōs hēmeroi;] In his gardens tame peacocks are kept. And book 16, ch. 2: Γίνονται δὲ καὶ ταὼς ἐν Ἰνδοῖς τῶν πανταχόθι μέγιστοι. [Ginontai de kai taōs en Indois tōn pantachothi megistoi.] There are also in India by far the largest peacocks. And Lucian in the Ship: Ὄρνις ἐκ Φάσιδος, καὶ ταὼς ἐξ Ἰνδίας. [Ornis ek Phasidos, kai taōs ex Indias.] A fowl from the Phasis (the pheasant), and a peacock from India. [II, 844] Therefore, when Menodotus of Samos writes of peacocks, Πρώτιστοι καὶ ἐγένοντο, καὶ ἐτράφησαν ἐν Σάμῳ, καὶ ἐντεῦθεν εἰς τοὺς ἔξω τόπους διεδόθησαν, ὡς καὶ οἱ ἀλεκτρυόνες ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ αἱ καλούμεναι μελεαγρίδες ἐν τῇ Αἰτωλίᾳ· [col. 243] [Prōtistoi kai egenonto, kai etraphēsan en Samō, kai enteuthen eis tous exō topous diedothēsan, hōs kai hoi alektryones en tē Perside, kai hai kaloumenai meleagrides en tē Aitōlia;] They were first born and reared in Samos, and from there spread into other regions, as cocks from Persia, and the so-called guinea fowl from Aetolia: there is no doubt that he lies to flatter his own people. And it is objected in vain that there is an ancient fable about Argus, killed by Mercury and changed into a peacock. For the history or fable that ascribes the slaying of Argus to Mercury must be very ancient, since from it Mercury is called Ἀργειφόντης [Argeiphontēs] by Homer and Hesiod; but the metamorphosis of Argus into a peacock is a recent invention, and I find no author of it older than Moschus. Thus Apollodorus, roughly contemporary with Moschus, in book 2 of the Library, relates the slaying of Argus by Mercury without a γρῦ [gry] about his metamorphosis; nor does the old Scholiast of Homer on Iliad β′ [2] at the word Ἀργειφόντης [Argeiphontēs]. From this it appears that this fable was new and not widely accepted. Yet from it, once it arose, peacocks at last began to be regarded as the bird of Juno, to be attached by the poets to the goddess's chariot, to be kept in her temple at Samos, and even to be struck on the coins of the Samians, which survive to this day. I am not unaware that the Scholiast of Aristophanes holds that this fable is alluded to when, in the Birds, Euelpides says to the Hoopoe,
